composition.story: Magma sits deep under high pressure with gas dissolved in it. As it rises, pressure drops and the gas forms bubbles that swell. Step through four states to see the gas share of volume grow until it blasts the magma out.

aha.observation: As magma rises and pressure falls from 130 to 0.1 MPa, gas grows to about 90% of its volume and blasts it out.

states.label: Magma stored
states.sentence: Deep in the magma chamber, high pressure keeps the gas dissolved in the liquid rock.
states.why: At 130 MPa the gas stays dissolved, so no bubbles exist yet.

states.label: Magma rises
states.sentence: Buoyant magma pushes up the conduit. Pressure around it falls, and the first gas bubbles appear.
states.why: Lower pressure means the dissolved gas can no longer stay in the liquid.

states.label: Bubbles swell
states.sentence: Near the surface the bubbles expand sharply. The frothy magma takes up far more room and speeds up.
states.why: Gas volume rises as pressure drops, so the mixture accelerates upward.

states.label: Eruption
states.sentence: Bubbles take over and shatter the magma into ash. The gas blasts it out of the vent as a plume.
states.why: At about 90% gas, the magma fragments and the expanding gas drives the eruption.
